summary: This document defines security requirements for time protocols, focusing on PTP and NTP. It also discusses the security impact of time protocol practices and the performance implications of security mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: Network clocks can be misled by forged, altered, repeated, or delayed time messages. This RFC lists what security mechanisms for NTP and PTP need to protect. It does not specify a particular mechanism.

subtitle: Requirements for protecting NTP and PTP time exchanges from tampering.

tldr.problem: A compromised time source can give false time to systems that depend on network synchronization. Time protocols also face spoofing, replay, packet delay, and rogue-master attacks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7384 analyzes threats to NTP and PTP and states requirements for any security mechanism, including authentication, integrity, replay protection, fresh keys, and modes for secured and unsecured clocks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines requirements, not a security protocol. It also explains trade-offs between clock accuracy, intermediate-clock behavior, and security protection.

today: RFC 7384 is Informational and defines security requirements rather than a protocol. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Shared Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC focuses on the Network Time Protocol (NTP) and the Precision Time Protocol (PTP). It includes PTP even though PTP was not defined by the IETF, because both protocols are common ways to distribute time.

To discuss both protocols, it uses master for an NTP server or PTP master and slave for an NTP client or PTP slave. An intermediate clock receives time from a master and passes it onward.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC covers NTP and PTP and gives their time sources and receivers shared names. It sets requirements for security mechanisms rather than defining one.

sections.title: Threats to Time Protocols
sections.content:
An attacker may be inside a trusted network or outside it. A man-in-the-middle can intercept and change packets; a packet injector can send packets and may replay recorded multicast traffic.

The RFC analyzes attacks including packet manipulation, spoofing, replay, rogue-master selection, packet removal, delay manipulation, denial of service, and attacks on the grandmaster's external time source. A compromised time source can appear to work while delivering inaccurate time.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can impersonate a clock, alter or replay a message, or delay it. Each attack can make a system's time inaccurate or make the time service unavailable.

sections.title: Core Security Requirements
sections.content:
Any security mechanism must support authentication and authorization, protect packet integrity, prevent spoofing and replay, refresh keys, and avoid significantly degrading time-transfer quality. It must also provide a way to protect clock accuracy from man-in-the-middle delay or interception attacks.

For PTP, the RFC requires authentication of Announce and Management messages. It says denial-of-service mitigation and security associations for unicast and multicast should be supported; confidentiality is optional because timing information is usually not secret.
sections.plainLanguage: The required protections establish which clocks may participate and whether time messages have changed or been replayed. The mechanism must also preserve the quality of time transfer.

sections.title: Secure and Hybrid Modes
sections.content:
A security mechanism must support secure mode, in which a clock discards protocol packets from unsecured clocks. The RFC recommends hybrid mode as an option for gradual deployment, allowing secured and unsecured clocks to participate.

In hybrid mode, a master should be secured, and a secured slave should discard packets from unsecured clocks. The RFC notes that the described NTPv4 Autokey scheme does not meet this behavior when a less secure server has a more accurate clock.
sections.plainLanguage: Secure mode accepts time messages only from secured clocks. Hybrid mode can support a gradual transition, but secured slaves should still reject messages from unsecured clocks.

sections.title: Timing, Intermediate Clocks, and Other Security Services
sections.content:
When a protocol inserts a timestamp during transmission, encryption or integrity protection must be applied after the timestamp is added. Security processing can add unpredictable delay, which may reduce timing accuracy.

Intermediate clocks create a trade-off: hop-by-hop security lets them adjust time packets, while end-to-end protection limits their ability to change packets. The RFC also notes that other security services, including certificate validation, depend on synchronized clocks, while key distribution is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Security processing must account for timestamps and the delay it can add. Intermediate clocks can help timing accuracy but complicate end-to-end protection.
